full_text:
Interviewer:	Ok we’re looking at all women engineering, well women engineering students in their 2nd years really. We’re looking at whether they’re going on placement or not and why or why aren’t they going on placement? What are they expecting to get out of their placement and things like that and we’re hoping to look at the influences on women’s career intentions and what they expect the industry’s going to be like and we hope to compare it to what they actually think once they get into industry see if there’s anything we can do to improve the situation for women in engineering really.

Subject:	OK

Interviewer:	So before I start, you’re doing mechanical engineering?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	Ok. What A levels did you do?

Subject:	Maths, physics, economics and general studies.

Interviewer:	Ok, what type of school did you go to?

Subject:	Well, I actually repeated A levels. First I went to a normal comprehensive, repeated 2 at private college.

Interviewer:	OK, Ok did you find a difference in the 2 types of schools?

Subject:	Definitely.

Interviewer:	Was there a particular reason why?

Subject:	I went from 2 A’s in maths and physics to 2 B’s.

Interviewer:	Wow.

Subject:	I kind of (?)

Interviewer:	Yeah, Ok, have you got any work experience?

Subject:	Yes, the first one is 2 weeks at [company] (OK) I then did a summer job at a company building dashboards for [company]. That’s – erm, I worked at a car track as well, I suppose that’s a kind of engineering.

Interviewer:	Everything’s experience. What do your parents do, are they engineers?

Subject:	My dad used to be an engineer, my mum does various things. She’s got her own company but she’s also a school inspector.

Interviewer:	OK when and why do you think that you decided to study engineering?

Subject:	Erm, when I was at school, the careers people said what are your favourite subjects? I said maths and physics, and they said, OK look at engineering and I said, no. I’d never looked at it and I’d – it just didn’t interest me, but one day I looked at a prospectus and it looked it really good. I also did EMTA engineering course for girls, that kind of confirmed that mechanical was the better one for me.

Interviewer:	Do you think that you ruled engineering out, to begin with, because you didn’t really know what it was?

Subject:	Definitely. I’d never looked at it before – I just for some reason, I thought no. I just didn’t know enough about it.

Interviewer:	OK, what factors do you think did influence your decision so was it like careers advisors and careers literature, that was obviously quite a big influence – what about your family, were they supportive?

Subject:	Yeah, they supported me whatever I wanted to do because even when I wanted to be a vet.

Interviewer:	Bit different;

Subject:	Yes, and no, but the chemistry put me off that. (OK) But they supported me through that, when I changed to engineering same again, so I didn’t really change my mind at all.

Interviewer:	OK, was there anything specific on the engineering course that you did that made you think mechanical engineering?

Subject:	The EMTA one?

Interviewer:	Yeah.

Subject:	Erm, well it was at [university] so most of it was electronics and robotics and that didn’t particularly interest me but I can’t remember, there was one small lecture on mechanical – there wasn’t much, but it was so much more interesting. I can’t remember what it was because it was a long time ago.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that the course in itself helped you quite a lot to decide to come into engineering at university?

Subject:	I suppose I’d already decided, at that point, that I wanted to do engineering you know. That just kind of confirmed it and sort of put me off [university] as well.

Interviewer:	Did you do much career research? Did you know any engineers to talk to about their experiences or anything like that?

Subject:	No. 

Interviewer:	What is it specifically that you think appeals to you about engineering?

Subject:	Erm, at [this university] not a lot (laughing)

Interviewer:	OK. 

Subject:	Erm, I quite like the design side of things but I don’t actually enjoy drawing things, I just like to be able to design it, if I was good at drawing (OK) I’d like that side of it.
Problem solving as well, I guess.

Interviewer:	Are you going on a placement?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	Have you got a placement?

Subject:	Not yet.

Interviewer:	Why do you think that you decided to do a sandwich course then?

Subject:	Again, the experience. I’ve got a friend who’s gone straight to her 3rd year and she’s really struggling to find a place – (really) all companies are saying that she hasn’t got that year of experience, so she is struggling. So I’m glad I’m actually going to do it.

Interviewer:	OK, how did you decide to come to [this] University?

Subject:	Erm, I’d already heard that [this university] was good but I did ask [company], [company] and [company] erm which course and where they suggested, and they said do mechanical, not automotive and go to [this university], because that’s where they get most of their students from.

Interviewer:	Oh right, that’s interesting. So did you consider doing automotive then?

Subject:	I had considered it, yes, but thought mechanical would be a better idea.

Interviewer:	Why do you think that the companies prefer mechanical?

Subject:	It’s more diverse, they can move them around a bit more as well. Automotive’s a bit too focussed.

Interviewer:	OK, when you decided to do engineering did you realise that it was so male dominated?

Subject:	Yeah, but I’d done physics which was loads of guys so it didn’t really bother me. I’ve got 2 brothers so.

Interviewer:	Do you think that more women should be encouraged to take engineering?

Subject:	Well then it could be competitive for me then, so no (laughter). Yeah, they’ve actually got a few girls as it is at [this university], so it doesn’t really – it’s not that noticeable. The guys find it noticeable but I don’t.

Interviewer:	Ok, so it doesn’t really feel like an issue for you?

Subject:	No, not really, in some ways it’s better.

Interviewer:	Yeah, I was going to ask about that do you think that there are advantages to being a woman in engineering?

Subject:	Mm, yeah there definitely are.

Interviewer:	What types of things?

Subject:	You can be – act stupid if you don’t know something and don’t get told off. Actually, [company] was a good place for women, because I was in an area that they were building engines they’d done research on and sort of innovating and all that. They’re all built by guys on the shop floor but they’re all designed by women in the design team upstairs (right) and, as regards, we had 2 engines on the go – both for women. It wasn’t unusual, at [company], to have women around, so it was quite good.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that anything could be done, at an early stage, say in education, to encourage more women into engineering?

Subject:	Erm, I suppose a bit more knowledge of actually what it is, because you do things at school but you don’t necessarily know these things are engineering – you think it’s science (yes). So I suppose a bit more emphasis that this is actually engineering that you’re doing would probably be better, then I would have known that what I found fun, was engineering.

Interviewer:	OK, why do you think that more women don’t do engineering?

Subject:	I don’t know. I suppose they see it as hands on, dirty sort of job and lots of guys that are ugly, which is true. 

Interviewer:	So again you think it’s about being provided with the right information probably?

Subject:	Mm, I was waiting for an exam on one occasion, when I overheard somebody else on another course saying, oh they’ll be engineers, just look at them. I thought blooming heck.

Interviewer:	I’m going to ask you a bit about your actual course now and your experiences on your course – what did you expect to get from your degree, like in terms of the skills that you’ve been taught and the type of teaching that you’ve had. Probably gender proportions – anything really, is it what you expected it would be?

Subject:	I suppose I expected less women on the course. 

Interviewer:	How many are there? What is the sort of proportion?

Subject:	I think it started about 17. I suppose it was out of 160 at that time, it’s now out of about 140, there’s probably 14 or something like that. So it’s gone down but not a huge amount.

Interviewer:	And what have been the best and worst things about the course so far?

Subject:	Erm, the worst is having lecturers that can’t speak proper English. When you can’t understand. Like the Russians – they have to be the worst understand and listen to. They can put you to sleep in less than 5 minutes.

Interviewer:	Oh that is quite a big issue as well, isn’t it, because you feel like you can’t complain because you don’t want to….

Subject:	Yeah, well it’s not exactly something they can put right – they can’t give elocution lessons. So, it’s like, it takes you a while to figure out what they’ve said and by the time you’ve figured out what they’ve said and like, then translated it into normal English, they’ve already gone ahead 2 sentences and you – it’s like, oh forget it.

Interviewer:	What is the best thing?

Subject:	Now that’s gonna make me think (laughter).

Interviewer:	There must be something.

Subject:	Erm, I suppose there are some good lecturers around that you can just sit and listen to and just take it on board. There are some good ones so – Group work tends to be quite good as well, if you get the right group. I’ve had mostly good groups actually.

Interviewer:	 (?) group?

Subject:	Well the IBDP group had absolutely no arguments whatsoever through the whole year, it was good.

Interviewer:	How do you decide who to work with in groups? Do you get told or..?

Subject:	We could have chosen but I didn’t – I was just put with a group. It was completely random (OK) but it was a good group.

Interviewer:	And what was the sort of mix of that group – male and female?

Subject:	I was the only girl. I think that helped actually.

Interviewer:	Helped in what way?

Subject:	I think girls are more likely to argue. My house mate was with a girl and she had so many arguments and felt so depressed through it all, it just wasn’t worth it. She still hates – they still hate each other now. She kind of deserved it to be fair, but …

Interviewer:	Would you rather work with people that you don’t know, than friends because of things like that?

Subject:	Definitely, definitely. I think a lot of people say it’s better, especially girls – I think it’s different for guys – I think they get along better, but for girls I think it’s better to work with strangers, rather than friends. It’s like living with them – you’re bound to end up not friends at the end of it.

Interviewer:	Yes, I know about that. Have you had any particular bad experiences then of working in groups?

Subject:	Not particularly, no –usually – ‘cos I’ve already been with a group of guys and they’re usually easy going, but its sort of me being the girl, so.

Interviewer:	Yeah, they’re quite accepting?

Subject:	Yeah, it’s quite int – it’s quite good actually.

Interviewer:	OK, have you been taught by male and female lecturers?

Subject:	Erm, well I’m actually repeating part B and up to last year, when I did first time part B, I had no female lecturers, but this time, repeating one of the modules there is a female, for the first time.

Interviewer:	OK, is their teaching style any different to the male lecturers, do you think?

Subject:	Yeah, I think that – well, she’s a good lecturer but I think the guys give her a bit of stick for it.

Interviewer:	Really?

Subject:	Yeah. 

Interviewer:	Does she treat the males and females the same?

Subject:	I think so. She’s my tutor as well.

Interviewer:	Oh right, OK.

Subject:	I kind of know her in a different light. She’s a really good tutor – she’s probably a better tutor than a lecturer. (OK) But I’ve also got another tutor, ‘cos she’s off on maternity leave at the moment, which is why I didn’t have her last year because she was having the first child.

Interviewer:	OK, I see. Do you think that female and male lecturers treat the woman students the same?

Subject:	I can’t really answer for her ‘cos I haven’t really come across that, but for the male lecturers – certain ones you can get round your little finger if you get the right bloke. That’s an advantage I think.

Interviewer:	No disadvantages then?

Subject:	No, not usually – apart from the ones that are just nasty to everyone.

Interviewer:	OK, who or what do you think has been the biggest influence on you since you started your degree?

Subject:	I don’t think there is anything.

Interviewer:	OK that’s fine. Do you think there are any particular aspects of university teaching, or advice that you’ve had, that will help you on your placement?

Subject:	No. 

Interviewer:	What about any particular skills from the course that you might take to the placement with you?

Subject:	Er, first year was the (sugar cube) project, that we had to actually make the thing – so we had hands on experience there.

Interviewer:	Yes, do you think there should be more hands on work?

Subject:	It’s a bit time consuming, so probably the one is enough, ‘cos it does take a long time and they try and shove a huge project into a short time and it just gets annoying. So I think that one of those is enough.

Interviewer:	Yeah, do you think that group work – can that type of work help in the more generic type of skills like the communication skills and that?

Subject:	If it was in the 2nd year, yes, but in the 1st year people are not quite mature enough, I think, to really use the opportunity (yes). So I think the good (?) they’re a bit immature to be honest.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that maybe the previous work experience that you’ve had, will help more than the course, when you do go on your work placement?

Subject:	Yes. I would say so. The one with the dashboards, I was actually responsible for people making what I’d designed so that’s a much better experience than what I’ve had here, because it’s a working atmosphere. It also looks good on the CV.

Interviewer:	OK, do you feel prepared and ready to go on placement at this time? Like you said, after the first year people were probably still a bit immature and it wouldn’t have been right to go on placement at the end of the first year probably, but do you feel like you’re ready now?

Subject:	I am now but I don’t know whether I was last year – for the first time in Part B, I don’t think I was quite there then but I – I suppose I’ve got more spare time now, so I do feel more ready now.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that the university’s done anything to help prepare you for the work place?

Subject:	No.

Interviewer:	Do you think that they could?

Subject:	Erm, we’ve actually had no off-site visits at all – I know some of the groups get that, but only a visit to a company of some sort. I’ve heard actually that they take us to [name] power station, which apparently is a really boring trip but – but still. So maybe something like that would be good.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that your educational experience and the way that you’ve been taught, reflects what it’s really like in the engineering industry?

Subject:	In University?

Interviewer:	Yeah.

Subject:	No, not at all. Er, the whole atmosphere is a kind of step between school and work but it’s neither one or the other. 

Interviewer:	Yeah, do you think that it should be like that or it should be different?

Subject:	I think it could be a bit more like a working atmosphere and they say the lecturers are like more easy going than what you get at school for teachers but they’re still higher up than us and it still shows, so I think it could be a bit more of a working atmosphere.

Interviewer:	Yeah, Ok. Did anyone particularly encourage you or discourage you to go on the work placement?

Subject:	Er, no. I was questioning whether to do it after this year, with repeating a year. And, I spoke to my tutor and he didn’t push me one way or the other, he just put the facts down straight and helped me decide for myself, which was good. So I eventually decided that it probably would be a good idea. Also, having heard about my house mate, from last year, who’s struggling – it certainly decided my mind.

Interviewer:	OK. I think you said you don’t know where you’re going yet – how did you decide what types of company to apply to?

Subject:	Erm, well [placement co-ordinator] will send emails saying about companies and what you’re doing and you just look and think, does that interest me? Things like [company] or power generation, they really don’t interest me, so they go straight into the recycle bin. But, the automotive ones or you know, something a bit different, then I would actually apply to. Like [company], I’ve had an interview with them.

Interviewer:	OK, so is it fair to say that the thing that attracts you to companies, is the actual type of work that you are likely to be dealing with, the type of work that they as a company do?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Did you consider things like pay and training opportunities and longer term career prospects?

Subject:	Erm, I don’t normally look at the pay and they don’t always show what the training is, but the long term thing I guess I’m interested in, so that if I do go back afterwards I’m actually going somewhere I like, so.

Interviewer:	OK, did you do much research into the companies that you’ve applied to?

Subject:	Only to find out the sorts of things that they’re doing. Maybe a bit more if I’m going to interview. I’ll find out a bit more but not huge amounts.

Interviewer:	And have you had any interviews yet?

Subject:	I’ve had 3.

Interviewer:	OK and you’re waiting to hear from them at the minute?

Subject:	2 of them have turned me down, 1 I’m waiting.

Interviewer:	OK. I think that you said that university has been quite helpful in helping people find placements and providing you with the list of companies, (yeah) do you think that they could provide any more help at all?

Subject:	 [the placement co-ordinator] always bombards our email box, there’s like 6 a day, 10 a day, it’s really silly.

Interviewer:	OK, did you ever consider getting sponsored to do the course? Was that an option for you?

Subject:	Yes, but – I looked at whilst doing ‘A’ levels but doing ‘A’ levels, I didn’t have much time to write in, but I have considered it yeah.

Interviewer:	Ok, do you think there are any particular advantages or disadvantages in being sponsored?

Subject:	Money. It’s as simple as that and I suppose if you get the right company they give you a placement as well.

Interviewer:	Yeah. Do you think there are disadvantages?

Subject:	If you decided that you’d changed your mind. Because I – at one point – wanted to do sort of automotive, sort of in the car industry, but I’ve now changed my mind and I don’t particularly want to go into that industry because a lot of the companies tend to be a bit snobbish. Not all of them. [Company’s] actually OK, but some of the others like [company], they’re just – I wouldn’t want to go to. So if I’d have got sponsored by someone like [company] I would have hated it but I would have been stuck.

Interviewer:	OK, what are you really expecting to get out of your placement?

Subject:	Erm, money and a bit of experience in the working atmosphere.

Interviewer:	Yeah, do you think that you’ll get an opportunity to put what you’ve learnt at university, into practice more?

Subject:	I think so. I don’t know quite how ‘cos what we do at university doesn’t seem like engineering to me, or actually worthwhile at all but apparently it does actually come in useful, so…

Interviewer:	Is the course not what you expected in that respect then?

Subject:	No, not at all.

Interviewer:	OK

Subject:	I don’t know what I expected but I didn’t expect this.

Interviewer:	OK, what do you think will be the worst and the best things about going on placement?

Subject:	Erm, being a bit more in charge of things because here you’re told what to do a bit. If you work in a company you’re a bit more in charge yourself, and also getting money. Definitely.

Interviewer:	What about the worst things?

Subject:	Finding a company that – where they give you something that you don’t like and you can’t do and they can’t be bothered to tell you how to do it.

Interviewer:	OK, how do you expect that work will differ from university?

Subject:	Erm, well I guess you have to be a bit more in charge of what you do rather than guided through it.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the actual skills that you are using will be different?

Subject:	Erm, I don’t know to be honest.

Interviewer:	OK, that’s fine. In terms of your career then, where do you see yourself in 5 years time?

Subject:	Probably not doing engineering.

Interviewer:	Really?

Subject:	I don’t know it depends how the year out goes. If that inspires me then yeah, I’ll stay, but other than that, it’s a degree at the end of the day.

Interviewer:	Is that – is that one of the reasons then why you are doing this year out, to sort of confirm in your own mind whether engineering is or isn’t for you?

Subject:	No, I’m probably doing the year out – partly for the money, but also it gives me a bit more creditation, sort of on my degree. That’s probably the only reasons (OK) because it’s actually a scary thought going out to work for a year.

Interviewer:	Is it?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	In what way?

Subject:	Never knowing quite what to expect. Whether they expect you to know loads of things that you’ve been taught. It’s like ‘you were taught that’, was I? So it’s actually quite scary.

Interviewer:	OK, what do you think then would be your ideal career?

Subject:	I don’t know I keep changing, so I haven’t really got a definite anymore. It used to be designing cars so that erm I’d sort of walk down the street and someone drives past in a car you’ve designed and somebody’s bought, and you’ve liked something I designed, it’d be cool. Erm, I suppose that’d still be the thing, but I don’t think I’ll actually get there.

Interviewer:	Why?

Subject:	Partly it means design work – which I’m no good at – but I just think it’s too competitive and I don’t think I’ll actually get there.

Interviewer:	Do you think that it is a competitive industry because it is so male dominated?

Subject:	Yes, and that’s probably why I ended up not liking car companies, because they don’t care.

Interviewer:	OK, what do you think you’re going to do next and how do you decide what to do? How do you think you’ll reach the decision?

Subject:	Erm, well at the moment I’m just applying to the companies that look interesting. Eventually I’ll get one er see how that goes and if it interests me, then I might decide it that way.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that the career prospects are good in engineering?

Subject:	No. a lot of people struggle to get a job after – when they finish, no matter whether they’ve had a year out or not and there’s now a lot of people that can’t find a job.

Interviewer:	What about once you’re actually in the industry? What about moving up?

Subject:	I haven’t really spoken to people about that.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think it would help if you did or – if you spoke to people with more experience?

Subject:	Possibly but they’re bound to say don’t do engineering. Go somewhere else.

Interviewer:	Do you think they are going to say that?

Subject:	I have known engineers say that to me, yeah. On the job with the dashboards – they’re saying you’re stupid, don’t do engineering.

Interviewer:	Why do you think that they were saying that?

Subject:	It wasn’t a good company for engineers to be in, to be honest, so that might be why. But, it isn’t what people expect, I think.

Interviewer:	OK, are you happy with all the career choices that you’ve made so far?

Subject:	Yes,

Interviewer:	Would you doing anything differently if you had to do it again?

Subject:	No.

Interviewer:	OK, are you happy that you came to Loughborough University?

Subject:	Yes, I want to stay here if I pass this year.

Interviewer:	What 5 words would you use to describe the culture or characteristics of the engineering industry?

Subject:	5 words?

Interviewer:	It doesn’t have to be the exact 5 words but if you had to use like descriptive words.

Subject:	It’s so varied you can’t really narrow it down. Some companies are still very old fashioned, male dominated, people that are nearing retirement and use a machine that’s about 50 years old, but other companies are – they’ve got brand new equipment that even the university wouldn’t consider getting – it’s just really new and very cutting edge and they tend to have more women, so it’s too varied to really narrow it down.

Interviewer:	When you’ve looked at companies have you quite considered that sort of thing then?

Subject:	Yeah, there was 1 company that er did diesel engines I think it was. Erm, my house mate applied to them last year – I didn’t realise – but she said that it was very male dominated old fogies, in groups, and they were really horrible.

Interviewer:	OK why did you think that the engineering culture is so masculine?

Subject:	Erm, I suppose it’s ‘cos it’s hand on and it’s sort of considered to be engines and cars, which are meant to be a guy thing. It’s what they’re pushed into. But I don’t see it as hugely male dominated because we’ve already said there’s women around, so it’s not that dominated by men.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that the situation will improve?

Subject:	Gradually I think it will. I don’t really know because I’ve only been through (sort of minor) – so I don’t know what people at school are being taught now. I can’t really say whether it should help.

Interviewer:	Do you think that any aspect with the engineering culture will be problematic for you?

Subject:	In what sort of way?

Interviewer:	Maybe in the fact that it is quite male dominated. Do you think that’ll have any impact upon you, in choosing what you want to do, if you do want to go into the industry?

Subject:	The companies that I tend to go for don’t really have an issue with male domination. For instance [company] it was – it seemed to be half and half. There was no bias one way or the other so it didn’t become an issue. So I can’t imagine that I’ll stay in the company very long if it is an issue but at most companies it’s not.

Interviewer:	And has that been a consideration when you have been applying to companies?

Subject:	I suppose sub-consciously when I go and visit them, make sure I look around. If they look at you as if – what are you doing here? Obviously, I’m not gonna like the company. So it kind of – I suppose it is an issue but not knowingly.

Interviewer:	OK, that’s fine yeah. Do you think that your educational experiences differ from other students, say in Social Sciences or business or things like that?

Subject:	Yeah, I think the year out is unusual on other courses. Most courses don’t have a year out and so that’s quite different.

Interviewer:	Good different?

Subject:	I hope so, yeah. It gives you a year – a break from studies. It also means that you’ve got to drag yourself back.

Interviewer:	Do you think it’ll difficult going back for the last year?

Subject:	I know a lot of people that say they don’t want to go back to Uni. There’s a guy who’s in Australia, at the moment, who’s taken a year out to stay there another year so. That was a good idea.

Interviewer:	That’s all the questions I’ve got to ask you…

Subject:	Apparently they needed a tutor to actually go and visit him.

Interviewer:	I bet they were all jumping to go weren’t they?

Subject:	Apparently, there was somebody already in the area – as you do…

Interviewer:	Obviously! OK, that’s it – thank you very much.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: My dad used to be an engineer, my mum does various things. She’s got her own company but she’s also a school inspector.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK when and why do you think that you decided to study engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, when I was at school, the careers people said what are your favourite subjects? I said maths and physics, and they said, OK look at engineering and I said, no. I’d never looked at it and I’d – it just didn’t interest me, but one day I looked at a prospectus and it looked it really good. I also did EMTA engineering course for girls, that kind of confirmed that mechanical was the better one for me.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that you ruled engineering out, to begin with, because you didn’t really know what it was?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Definitely. I’d never looked at it before – I just for some reason, I thought no. I just didn’t know enough about it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what factors do you think did influence your decision so was it like careers advisors and careers literature, that was obviously quite a big influence – what about your family, were they supportive?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, they supported me whatever I wanted to do because even when I wanted to be a vet.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Bit different;

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, and no, but the chemistry put me off that. (OK) But they supported me through that, when I changed to engineering same again, so I didn’t really change my mind at all.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, was there anything specific on the engineering course that you did that made you think mechanical engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: The EMTA one?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, well it was at [university] so most of it was electronics and robotics and that didn’t particularly interest me but I can’t remember, there was one small lecture on mechanical – there wasn’t much, but it was so much more interesting. I can’t remember what it was because it was a long time ago.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that the course in itself helped you quite a lot to decide to come into engineering at university?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I suppose I’d already decided, at that point, that I wanted to do engineering you know. That just kind of confirmed it and sort of put me off [university] as well.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you do much career research? Did you know any engineers to talk to about their experiences or anything like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What is it specifically that you think appeals to you about engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, at [this university] not a lot (laughing)

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I quite like the design side of things but I don’t actually enjoy drawing things, I just like to be able to design it, if I was good at drawing (OK) I’d like that side of it. Problem solving as well, I guess.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are you going on a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you got a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not yet.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why do you think that you decided to do a sandwich course then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Again, the experience. I’ve got a friend who’s gone straight to her 3rd year and she’s really struggling to find a place – (really) all companies are saying that she hasn’t got that year of experience, so she is struggling. So I’m glad I’m actually going to do it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, how did you decide to come to [this] University?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I’d already heard that [this university] was good but I did ask [company], [company] and [company] erm which course and where they suggested, and they said do mechanical, not automotive and go to [this university], because that’s where they get most of their students from.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Oh right, that’s interesting. So did you consider doing automotive then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I had considered it, yes, but thought mechanical would be a better idea.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why do you think that the companies prefer mechanical?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It’s more diverse, they can move them around a bit more as well. Automotive’s a bit too focussed.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, when you decided to do engineering did you realise that it was so male dominated?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, but I’d done physics which was loads of guys so it didn’t really bother me. I’ve got 2 brothers so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that more women should be encouraged to take engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well then it could be competitive for me then, so no (laughter). Yeah, they’ve actually got a few girls as it is at [this university], so it doesn’t really – it’s not that noticeable. The guys find it noticeable but I don’t.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, so it doesn’t really feel like an issue for you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, not really, in some ways it’s better.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, I was going to ask about that do you think that there are advantages to being a woman in engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Mm, yeah there definitely are.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What types of things?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: You can be – act stupid if you don’t know something and don’t get told off. Actually, [company] was a good place for women, because I was in an area that they were building engines they’d done research on and sort of innovating and all that. They’re all built by guys on the shop floor but they’re all designed by women in the design team upstairs (right) and, as regards, we had 2 engines on the go – both for women. It wasn’t unusual, at [company], to have women around, so it was quite good.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that anything could be done, at an early stage, say in education, to encourage more women into engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I suppose a bit more knowledge of actually what it is, because you do things at school but you don’t necessarily know these things are engineering – you think it’s science (yes). So I suppose a bit more emphasis that this is actually engineering that you’re doing would probably be better, then I would have known that what I found fun, was engineering.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, why do you think that more women don’t do engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t know. I suppose they see it as hands on, dirty sort of job and lots of guys that are ugly, which is true.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So again you think it’s about being provided with the right information probably?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Mm, I was waiting for an exam on one occasion, when I overheard somebody else on another course saying, oh they’ll be engineers, just look at them. I thought blooming heck.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: I’m going to ask you a bit about your actual course now and your experiences on your course – what did you expect to get from your degree, like in terms of the skills that you’ve been taught and the type of teaching that you’ve had. Probably gender proportions – anything really, is it what you expected it would be?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I suppose I expected less women on the course.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How many are there? What is the sort of proportion?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it started about 17. I suppose it was out of 160 at that time, it’s now out of about 140, there’s probably 14 or something like that. So it’s gone down but not a huge amount.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And what have been the best and worst things about the course so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, the worst is having lecturers that can’t speak proper English. When you can’t understand. Like the Russians – they have to be the worst understand and listen to. They can put you to sleep in less than 5 minutes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Oh that is quite a big issue as well, isn’t it, because you feel like you can’t complain because you don’t want to….

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, well it’s not exactly something they can put right – they can’t give elocution lessons. So, it’s like, it takes you a while to figure out what they’ve said and by the time you’ve figured out what they’ve said and like, then translated it into normal English, they’ve already gone ahead 2 sentences and you – it’s like, oh forget it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What is the best thing?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Now that’s gonna make me think (laughter).

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: There must be something.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I suppose there are some good lecturers around that you can just sit and listen to and just take it on board. There are some good ones so – Group work tends to be quite good as well, if you get the right group. I’ve had mostly good groups actually.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: (?) group?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well the IBDP group had absolutely no arguments whatsoever through the whole year, it was good.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How do you decide who to work with in groups? Do you get told or..?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: We could have chosen but I didn’t – I was just put with a group. It was completely random (OK) but it was a good group.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And what was the sort of mix of that group – male and female?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I was the only girl. I think that helped actually.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Helped in what way?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think girls are more likely to argue. My house mate was with a girl and she had so many arguments and felt so depressed through it all, it just wasn’t worth it. She still hates – they still hate each other now. She kind of deserved it to be fair, but …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you rather work with people that you don’t know, than friends because of things like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Definitely, definitely. I think a lot of people say it’s better, especially girls – I think it’s different for guys – I think they get along better, but for girls I think it’s better to work with strangers, rather than friends. It’s like living with them – you’re bound to end up not friends at the end of it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes, I know about that. Have you had any particular bad experiences then of working in groups?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not particularly, no –usually – ‘cos I’ve already been with a group of guys and they’re usually easy going, but its sort of me being the girl, so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, they’re quite accepting?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, it’s quite int – it’s quite good actually.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, have you been taught by male and female lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, well I’m actually repeating part B and up to last year, when I did first time part B, I had no female lecturers, but this time, repeating one of the modules there is a female, for the first time.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, is their teaching style any different to the male lecturers, do you think?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think that – well, she’s a good lecturer but I think the guys give her a bit of stick for it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Really?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Does she treat the males and females the same?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think so. She’s my tutor as well.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Oh right, OK.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I kind of know her in a different light. She’s a really good tutor – she’s probably a better tutor than a lecturer. (OK) But I’ve also got another tutor, ‘cos she’s off on maternity leave at the moment, which is why I didn’t have her last year because she was having the first child.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, I see. Do you think that female and male lecturers treat the woman students the same?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I can’t really answer for her ‘cos I haven’t really come across that, but for the male lecturers – certain ones you can get round your little finger if you get the right bloke. That’s an advantage I think.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: No disadvantages then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, not usually – apart from the ones that are just nasty to everyone.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, who or what do you think has been the biggest influence on you since you started your degree?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t think there is anything.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK that’s fine. Do you think there are any particular aspects of university teaching, or advice that you’ve had, that will help you on your placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What about any particular skills from the course that you might take to the placement with you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, first year was the (sugar cube) project, that we had to actually make the thing – so we had hands on experience there.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes, do you think there should be more hands on work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It’s a bit time consuming, so probably the one is enough, ‘cos it does take a long time and they try and shove a huge project into a short time and it just gets annoying. So I think that one of those is enough.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, do you think that group work – can that type of work help in the more generic type of skills like the communication skills and that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: If it was in the 2nd year, yes, but in the 1st year people are not quite mature enough, I think, to really use the opportunity (yes). So I think the good (?) they’re a bit immature to be honest.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that maybe the previous work experience that you’ve had, will help more than the course, when you do go on your work placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes. I would say so. The one with the dashboards, I was actually responsible for people making what I’d designed so that’s a much better experience than what I’ve had here, because it’s a working atmosphere. It also looks good on the CV.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you feel prepared and ready to go on placement at this time? Like you said, after the first year people were probably still a bit immature and it wouldn’t have been right to go on placement at the end of the first year probably, but do you feel like you’re ready now?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I am now but I don’t know whether I was last year – for the first time in Part B, I don’t think I was quite there then but I – I suppose I’ve got more spare time now, so I do feel more ready now.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that the university’s done anything to help prepare you for the work place?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that they could?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, we’ve actually had no off-site visits at all – I know some of the groups get that, but only a visit to a company of some sort. I’ve heard actually that they take us to [name] power station, which apparently is a really boring trip but – but still. So maybe something like that would be good.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that your educational experience and the way that you’ve been taught, reflects what it’s really like in the engineering industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: In University?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, not at all. Er, the whole atmosphere is a kind of step between school and work but it’s neither one or the other.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, do you think that it should be like that or it should be different?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it could be a bit more like a working atmosphere and they say the lecturers are like more easy going than what you get at school for teachers but they’re still higher up than us and it still shows, so I think it could be a bit more of a working atmosphere.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, Ok. Did anyone particularly encourage you or discourage you to go on the work placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, no. I was questioning whether to do it after this year, with repeating a year. And, I spoke to my tutor and he didn’t push me one way or the other, he just put the facts down straight and helped me decide for myself, which was good. So I eventually decided that it probably would be a good idea. Also, having heard about my house mate, from last year, who’s struggling – it certainly decided my mind.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. I think you said you don’t know where you’re going yet – how did you decide what types of company to apply to?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, well [placement co-ordinator] will send emails saying about companies and what you’re doing and you just look and think, does that interest me? Things like [company] or power generation, they really don’t interest me, so they go straight into the recycle bin. But, the automotive ones or you know, something a bit different, then I would actually apply to. Like [company], I’ve had an interview with them.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, so is it fair to say that the thing that attracts you to companies, is the actual type of work that you are likely to be dealing with, the type of work that they as a company do?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you consider things like pay and training opportunities and longer term career prospects?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I don’t normally look at the pay and they don’t always show what the training is, but the long term thing I guess I’m interested in, so that if I do go back afterwards I’m actually going somewhere I like, so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did you do much research into the companies that you’ve applied to?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Only to find out the sorts of things that they’re doing. Maybe a bit more if I’m going to interview. I’ll find out a bit more but not huge amounts.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And have you had any interviews yet?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’ve had 3.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK and you’re waiting to hear from them at the minute?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: 2 of them have turned me down, 1 I’m waiting.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. I think that you said that university has been quite helpful in helping people find placements and providing you with the list of companies, (yeah) do you think that they could provide any more help at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: [the placement co-ordinator] always bombards our email box, there’s like 6 a day, 10 a day, it’s really silly.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did you ever consider getting sponsored to do the course? Was that an option for you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, but – I looked at whilst doing ‘A’ levels but doing ‘A’ levels, I didn’t have much time to write in, but I have considered it yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, do you think there are any particular advantages or disadvantages in being sponsored?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Money. It’s as simple as that and I suppose if you get the right company they give you a placement as well.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. Do you think there are disadvantages?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: If you decided that you’d changed your mind. Because I – at one point – wanted to do sort of automotive, sort of in the car industry, but I’ve now changed my mind and I don’t particularly want to go into that industry because a lot of the companies tend to be a bit snobbish. Not all of them. [Company’s] actually OK, but some of the others like [company], they’re just – I wouldn’t want to go to. So if I’d have got sponsored by someone like [company] I would have hated it but I would have been stuck.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what are you really expecting to get out of your placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, money and a bit of experience in the working atmosphere.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, do you think that you’ll get an opportunity to put what you’ve learnt at university, into practice more?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think so. I don’t know quite how ‘cos what we do at university doesn’t seem like engineering to me, or actually worthwhile at all but apparently it does actually come in useful, so…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is the course not what you expected in that respect then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, not at all.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t know what I expected but I didn’t expect this.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what do you think will be the worst and the best things about going on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, being a bit more in charge of things because here you’re told what to do a bit. If you work in a company you’re a bit more in charge yourself, and also getting money. Definitely.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What about the worst things?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Finding a company that – where they give you something that you don’t like and you can’t do and they can’t be bothered to tell you how to do it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, how do you expect that work will differ from university?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, well I guess you have to be a bit more in charge of what you do rather than guided through it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the actual skills that you are using will be different?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I don’t know to be honest.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, that’s fine. In terms of your career then, where do you see yourself in 5 years time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Probably not doing engineering.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Really?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t know it depends how the year out goes. If that inspires me then yeah, I’ll stay, but other than that, it’s a degree at the end of the day.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is that – is that one of the reasons then why you are doing this year out, to sort of confirm in your own mind whether engineering is or isn’t for you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I’m probably doing the year out – partly for the money, but also it gives me a bit more creditation, sort of on my degree. That’s probably the only reasons (OK) because it’s actually a scary thought going out to work for a year.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is it?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: In what way?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Never knowing quite what to expect. Whether they expect you to know loads of things that you’ve been taught. It’s like ‘you were taught that’, was I? So it’s actually quite scary.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what do you think then would be your ideal career?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t know I keep changing, so I haven’t really got a definite anymore. It used to be designing cars so that erm I’d sort of walk down the street and someone drives past in a car you’ve designed and somebody’s bought, and you’ve liked something I designed, it’d be cool. Erm, I suppose that’d still be the thing, but I don’t think I’ll actually get there.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Partly it means design work – which I’m no good at – but I just think it’s too competitive and I don’t think I’ll actually get there.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that it is a competitive industry because it is so male dominated?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, and that’s probably why I ended up not liking car companies, because they don’t care.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what do you think you’re going to do next and how do you decide what to do? How do you think you’ll reach the decision?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, well at the moment I’m just applying to the companies that look interesting. Eventually I’ll get one er see how that goes and if it interests me, then I might decide it that way.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that the career prospects are good in engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No. a lot of people struggle to get a job after – when they finish, no matter whether they’ve had a year out or not and there’s now a lot of people that can’t find a job.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What about once you’re actually in the industry? What about moving up?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I haven’t really spoken to people about that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think it would help if you did or – if you spoke to people with more experience?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Possibly but they’re bound to say don’t do engineering. Go somewhere else.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think they are going to say that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I have known engineers say that to me, yeah. On the job with the dashboards – they’re saying you’re stupid, don’t do engineering.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why do you think that they were saying that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It wasn’t a good company for engineers to be in, to be honest, so that might be why. But, it isn’t what people expect, I think.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, are you happy with all the career choices that you’ve made so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes,

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you doing anything differently if you had to do it again?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, are you happy that you came to Loughborough University?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, I want to stay here if I pass this year.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What 5 words would you use to describe the culture or characteristics of the engineering industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: 5 words?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: It doesn’t have to be the exact 5 words but if you had to use like descriptive words.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It’s so varied you can’t really narrow it down. Some companies are still very old fashioned, male dominated, people that are nearing retirement and use a machine that’s about 50 years old, but other companies are – they’ve got brand new equipment that even the university wouldn’t consider getting – it’s just really new and very cutting edge and they tend to have more women, so it’s too varied to really narrow it down.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: When you’ve looked at companies have you quite considered that sort of thing then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, there was 1 company that er did diesel engines I think it was. Erm, my house mate applied to them last year – I didn’t realise – but she said that it was very male dominated old fogies, in groups, and they were really horrible.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK why did you think that the engineering culture is so masculine?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I suppose it’s ‘cos it’s hand on and it’s sort of considered to be engines and cars, which are meant to be a guy thing. It’s what they’re pushed into. But I don’t see it as hugely male dominated because we’ve already said there’s women around, so it’s not that dominated by men.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that the situation will improve?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Gradually I think it will. I don’t really know because I’ve only been through (sort of minor) – so I don’t know what people at school are being taught now. I can’t really say whether it should help.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that any aspect with the engineering culture will be problematic for you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: In what sort of way?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Maybe in the fact that it is quite male dominated. Do you think that’ll have any impact upon you, in choosing what you want to do, if you do want to go into the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: The companies that I tend to go for don’t really have an issue with male domination. For instance [company] it was – it seemed to be half and half. There was no bias one way or the other so it didn’t become an issue. So I can’t imagine that I’ll stay in the company very long if it is an issue but at most companies it’s not.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And has that been a consideration when you have been applying to companies?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I suppose sub-consciously when I go and visit them, make sure I look around. If they look at you as if – what are you doing here? Obviously, I’m not gonna like the company. So it kind of – I suppose it is an issue but not knowingly.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, that’s fine yeah. Do you think that your educational experiences differ from other students, say in Social Sciences or business or things like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think the year out is unusual on other courses. Most courses don’t have a year out and so that’s quite different.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Good different?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I hope so, yeah. It gives you a year – a break from studies. It also means that you’ve got to drag yourself back.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it’ll difficult going back for the last year?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I know a lot of people that say they don’t want to go back to Uni. There’s a guy who’s in Australia, at the moment, who’s taken a year out to stay there another year so. That was a good idea.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That’s all the questions I’ve got to ask you…

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Apparently they needed a tutor to actually go and visit him.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: I bet they were all jumping to go weren’t they?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Apparently, there was somebody already in the area – as you do…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Obviously! OK, that’s it – thank you very much.
